```{r helpers, echo=FALSE}
# scientific workflow schematic; 'highlight' shades one box
draw_workflow <- function(highlight = NULL, cex = 0.9) {
  boxes <- c("PROBLEM", "THEORIES", "MODELS", "FIT", "COMPARE")
  subs <- c("what do we\nneed to know?", "candidate\nexplanations",
            "data-generating\n(process + noise)", "confront each\nwith data",
            "fit, prediction,\nrelevance")
  x <- seq(1, 9, by = 2)
  y <- 2
  w <- 0.8
  h <- 0.55
  shade <- function(lab) if (!is.null(highlight) && lab == highlight) "lightskyblue1" else "white"
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(-0.2, 4), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_along(boxes)) {
    rect(x[i] - w, y - h, x[i] + w, y + h, col = shade(boxes[i]), lwd = 1.5)
    text(x[i], y + 0.18, boxes[i], font = 2, cex = cex)
    text(x[i], y - 0.22, subs[i], cex = cex * 0.75)
  }
  arrows(x[-5] + w, y, x[-1] - w, y, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  rect(6 - 0.7, 3.2 - 0.35, 6 + 0.7, 3.2 + 0.35, lty = 2, lwd = 1.5,
       col = if (identical(highlight, "DATA")) "lightskyblue1" else NA)
  text(6, 3.28, "DATA", font = 2, cex = cex)
  text(6, 3.0, "study design", cex = cex * 0.75)
  arrows(x[3], y + h, 6 - 0.7, 3.2, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  arrows(6 + 0.7, 3.2, x[4], y + h, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  segments(x[5], y - h, x[5], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  segments(x[5], 0.4, x[1], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  arrows(x[c(1, 2)], 0.4, x[c(1, 2)], y - h, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  text(6, 0.15, "REVISE the problem and theories; drop or down-weight poor models",
       cex = cex * 0.85, font = 3)
}

# bar chart of a pmf with the mean marked by a triangle under the axis
pmf_plot <- function(x, p, xlab, main = "", col = "grey60", ylim = NULL) {
  mids <- barplot(p, names.arg = x, col = col, border = NA, ylim = ylim,
                  xlab = xlab, ylab = "Probability", main = main)
  mu <- sum(x * p)
  pos <- approx(x, mids, xout = mu)$y
  points(pos, 0, pch = 17, cex = 1.6, col = "firebrick", xpd = TRUE)
  invisible(mids)
}
```

R code from this page is also in the
[companion script](lecture_notes/CODE_Week4_ProbabilityDistributions.R).
No packages beyond base R are needed.

This material follows Bolker, *Ecological Models and Data in R*,
sections 4.4 (analyzing probability distributions, pp. 155-160), 4.5
(the bestiary of distributions, pp. 160-182), and 4.6 (compounding
distributions, pp. 182-188). Factorials are in Appendix A.5 (p. 482).

# Counting, random variables, and expectation {#expectation}

Most of the distributions we use for ecological data are built from
two ingredients: counting the ways an outcome can happen, and
weighting each outcome by its probability. This part covers counting
(permutations, combinations, and the binomial coefficient), the
difference between a probability and a probability *density*, and the
two numbers that summarize a distribution most often: its expected
value and its variance.

## 1. Big picture

```{r workflow-models, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.8, dev="png", dpi=250}
draw_workflow("MODELS")
```

A data-generating model (MODELS) has two halves: a deterministic
function for the expected value, and a probability distribution for
the noise around it. Earlier weeks built the deterministic half (the
bestiary of functions). This week builds the noise half: what a
probability distribution is, how to summarize one, and which named
distributions fit which kinds of ecological data.

## 2. WOD: a probability puzzle {#wod-puzzle}

The WOD (a short warm-up exercise at the start of class) asked three
things: whether a sum of 7 or doubles is more likely when rolling two
dice; how many 5-number lottery tickets can be drawn from the numbers 1
to 30; and a guess at whether 25 people in a room are more likely than
not to share a birthday.

For the dice, list the sample space. Two dice that can be told apart
give $6 \times 6 = 36$ equally likely ordered pairs:

```{r dice-grid, echo=FALSE, fig.width=4.6, fig.height=4.4}
s <- outer(1:6, 1:6, "+")
par(mar = c(4, 4, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0.5, 6.5), ylim = c(0.5, 6.5), xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Blue die", ylab = "Red die", asp = 1)
axis(1, at = 1:6)
axis(2, at = 1:6, las = 1)
for (r in 1:6) for (b in 1:6) {
  fill <- if (s[r, b] == 7) "lightskyblue1" else if (r == b) "khaki1" else "white"
  rect(b - 0.5, r - 0.5, b + 0.5, r + 0.5, col = fill, border = "grey70")
  text(b, r, s[r, b], font = if (r == b) 3 else if (s[r, b] == 7) 2 else 1)
}
```

Six cells sum to 7 (blue, bold) and six are doubles (yellow, italic),
so both have probability $6/36 = 1/6$. Seven is the only sum that ties
doubles, because no other sum can be made in six ways.

> **Question:** With two eight-sided dice, which sum is most likely,
> and does it tie, beat, or lose to doubles?

The lottery and the birthday guess both need counting rules, which
come next.

## 3. Counting arrangements {#counting}

**Multiplication rule.** If one choice can be made in $a$ ways and a
second in $b$ ways, the pair can be made in $a \times b$ ways. The 36
dice outcomes are $6 \times 6$.

**Permutations (order matters).** A crew will resurvey 4 of 12 ponds
and must also decide the order of visits. There are 12 choices for the
first pond, 11 for the second, and so on:

$$12 \times 11 \times 10 \times 9 = \frac{12!}{8!}.$$

In general, the number of ordered selections of $k$ items from $N$ is

$$P(N, k) = \frac{N!}{(N - k)!}.$$

**Combinations (order doesn't matter).** If the crew only cares
*which* 4 ponds get visited, each set of 4 has been counted once for
each of its $4! = 24$ orderings. Divide that out:

$$\binom{N}{k} = \frac{P(N, k)}{k!} = \frac{N!}{k!\,(N - k)!}.$$

```{r counting}
12 * 11 * 10 * 9          # ordered visits
choose(12, 4)             # sets of 4 ponds
choose(30, 5)             # lottery tickets from the WOD
```

Forgetting to divide by $k!$ is the usual error. Ask: is
$\{3, 8, 14, 20, 29\}$ a different ticket from $\{29, 20, 14, 8, 3\}$?
If not, you need combinations.

### The binomial coefficient {#binomial-coefficient}

$\binom{N}{k}$ is read "$N$ choose $k$," and it is the
coefficient in the binomial probability mass function. Suppose each of
$N = 6$ nests fails independently with probability $p = 0.25$. One
particular outcome, say nests 1 and 4 fail and the rest hatch, has
probability

$$p^2 (1 - p)^4 = 0.25^2 \times 0.75^4.$$

But "2 of 6 failed" can happen in $\binom{6}{2} = 15$ different ways:

```{r nest-arrangements, echo=FALSE, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=3.6}
fails <- combn(6, 2)
par(mar = c(4, 1, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0.5, 6.5), ylim = c(0.5, 15.5), yaxt = "n", xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Nest", ylab = "", bty = "n")
axis(1, at = 1:6)
for (j in 1:15) {
  failed <- 1:6 %in% fails[, j]
  points(1:6, rep(16 - j, 6), pch = ifelse(failed, 4, 1),
         cex = 1.5, lwd = 2, col = ifelse(failed, "firebrick", "grey40"))
}
```

Each row is one arrangement (an X marks a failed nest), and each has
the same probability. Adding them up gives the binomial pmf:

$$P(X = k) = \binom{N}{k} p^k (1 - p)^{N - k}.$$

```{r nest-binomial}
choose(6, 2) * 0.25^2 * 0.75^4
dbinom(2, size = 6, prob = 0.25)
```

$\binom{N}{k}$ counts the arrangements; $p^k (1 - p)^{N - k}$ is the
probability of any one of them.

## 4. The birthday problem {#birthday}

Are 25 people more likely than not to include two who share a birthday?
Assume 365 equally likely birthdays and independence. "At least one
match" can happen in many ways (one pair, two pairs, three people on
one day), so compute its complement instead:

$$P(\text{at least one match}) = 1 - P(\text{all different}).$$

Assign birthdays one person at a time. Person 2 must avoid 1 taken
day, person 3 must avoid 2, and so on:

$$P(\text{all different}) = \frac{365}{365} \cdot \frac{364}{365}
\cdots \frac{341}{365} = \prod_{i=0}^{24} \frac{365 - i}{365}.$$

```{r birthday}
n_people <- 25
p_all_diff <- prod((365 - 0:(n_people - 1)) / 365)
1 - p_all_diff
choose(n_people, 2)
```

A shared birthday has probability `r f3(1 - p_all_diff)`. The intuitive
comparison, 25 people against 365 days, is the wrong one. What matters
is the number of *pairs*, since any pair can be the one that matches:
25 people make `r choose(n_people, 2)` pairs, each with a 1/365 chance.
For a rough rule, $P(\text{match}) \approx 1 - \exp(-\text{pairs} / 365)$.

The widget computes the exact probability for any group size and fills
simulated groups with random values. The buttons change the number of
equally likely values, for problems where the "days" are something
else (the genotypes in the discussion below, for example).

```{r birthday-widget, echo=FALSE}
widget("birthday.html")
```

> **Question:** With 365 values, find the smallest group with better
> than even odds of a match. How many pairs does it have? Switch to
> 10,000 values and find the smallest such group again. What do the
> two pair counts have in common?

## 5. Random variables and their distributions {#pmf-pdf}

A **random variable** is a rule that turns an outcome into a number:
the number of failed nests, the length of a trout, the pH of a pond. A
**probability distribution** says how likely each value is.

**Discrete random variables** take separate values, usually counts. A
**probability mass function** (pmf) gives $P(X = x)$ for each value,
and these probabilities sum to 1:

```{r nest-pmf}
x_nest <- 0:6
p_nest <- dbinom(x_nest, size = 6, prob = 0.25)
round(p_nest, 3)
sum(p_nest)
```

```{r nest-pmf-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 0.5, 0.5))
pmf_plot(x_nest, p_nest, xlab = "Failed nests (of 6)")
```

You can read a probability straight off the bar chart: $P(X = 2)$ is
the height of the third bar. The red triangle marks the distribution's
mean, 1.5 failed nests, which falls between two possible outcomes (see
[expectation and variance](#moments) below).

**Continuous random variables** take any value in a range. The chance
of any *exact* value is zero. Bolker's example (p. 156): a pH meter
reading "7.9" really says the pH is somewhere between 7.82 and 7.98.
So for continuous variables we describe probability per unit of $x$, a
**probability density** $f(x)$. Probabilities are areas under the
density curve:

$$P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\, dx.$$

Densities are not probabilities, and they can be larger than 1. If pH
is equally likely anywhere between 7.0 and 7.1 (and nowhere else), the
density is 10 per pH unit across that range, since the area
($10 \times 0.1$) must equal 1:

```{r ph-density}
dunif(7.05, min = 7.0, max = 7.1)
```

The **cumulative distribution function** (CDF), $F(x) = P(X \le x)$,
turns areas into differences: $P(a \le X \le b) = F(b) - F(a)$. For
brook trout lengths that are normal with mean 22 cm and SD 4 cm:

```{r trout-area}
pnorm(24, mean = 22, sd = 4) - pnorm(20, mean = 22, sd = 4)   # P(20 <= X <= 24)
dnorm(22, mean = 22, sd = 4)                                    # a density, per cm
```

A trout between 20 and 24 cm has probability
`r f3(pnorm(24, 22, 4) - pnorm(20, 22, 4))`. The value
`r f4(dnorm(22, 22, 4))` is the height of the density curve at 22 cm,
in units of probability per cm; it is not the probability that a trout
is 22 cm long.

The widget shades an interval under the trout density (left) and shows
the same probability as a gap in the CDF (right).

```{r density-widget, echo=FALSE}
widget("density_area.html")
```

> **Question:** Shrink the SD to about 0.1 cm. The curve now rises
> above a height of 1. Is the model broken? Then, at any SD, narrow the
> interval width toward zero and watch the "Area" and "Height ×
> width" cards. What happens to each, and what does that say about
> the probability of one exact length?

## 6. Expectation and variance {#moments}

**Expectation.** Suppose 40 survey routes each checked 6 nests and
recorded how many failed. The ordinary average of the 40 counts can be
computed from the tabulated counts $c(x)$ (Bolker eq. 4.4.2):

$$\bar{x} = \frac{\sum_i x_i}{N} = \sum_x x \, \frac{c(x)}{N}.$$

```{r tabulated-mean}
set.seed(4)
routes <- rbinom(40, size = 6, prob = 0.25)
counts <- table(factor(routes, levels = 0:6))
counts
mean(routes)
sum(0:6 * counts / 40)
```

Replace each observed frequency $c(x)/N$ with its probability, and the
average becomes the **expected value** of the distribution:

$$E[X] = \sum_x x \, P(X = x) \qquad\text{or}\qquad E[X] = \int x \, f(x)\, dx.$$

```{r expectation}
sum(x_nest * p_nest)                                     # binomial: N p = 1.5
integrate(function(x) x * dexp(x, rate = 1.5), 0, Inf)    # exponential: 1 / rate
```

$E[X]$ is a weighted average of the possible values, and it is the
balance point of the distribution: cut the bar chart above out of
cardboard and it balances on the red triangle. The sample mean (here
`r f3(mean(routes))`) is computed from data and varies from sample to
sample; $E[X]$ (here 1.5) is a fixed property of the distribution.

Expectation is linear. For constants $a$ and $b$ and any random
variables $X$ and $Y$,

$$E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b, \qquad E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y].$$

**Variance** is the expected squared distance from the mean,
$\text{Var}(X) = E[(X - \mu)^2]$ with $\mu = E[X]$. Expanding the square
and applying linearity gives a formula that is easier to compute:

$$\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2 - 2\mu X + \mu^2] = E[X^2] - 2\mu E[X] + \mu^2
= E[X^2] - \mu^2.$$

```{r variance}
mu_nest <- sum(x_nest * p_nest)
sum((x_nest - mu_nest)^2 * p_nest)       # E[(X - mu)^2]
sum(x_nest^2 * p_nest) - mu_nest^2       # E[X^2] - mu^2
6 * 0.25 * 0.75                          # binomial formula N p (1 - p)
```

Variance is in squared units (failed nests squared, cm²), so we often
report the **standard deviation** $\sqrt{\text{Var}(X)}$, or the
**coefficient of variation** $\text{CV} = \text{SD}/\text{mean}$. Shifting
a variable moves its mean but not its spread, and rescaling multiplies
the variance by the square of the factor:

$$\text{Var}(aX + b) = a^2 \, \text{Var}(X).$$

**Other summaries.** The mean is the first moment and the variance is
the second central moment. The third and fourth central moments
measure skewness (lopsidedness) and kurtosis (peakedness). The median
splits the probability in half and the mode is the most likely value.
For right-skewed distributions, generally mode < median < mean (Bolker
p. 159); for the nest distribution the mode is 1 and the mean is 1.5.

> **Question:** The expected number of failed nests is 1.5, but no
> survey can record 1.5 failures. In what sense is 1.5 "expected"?

## Discussion

1. A pond's pH is modeled as normal with mean 7.9 and SD 0.02. The
   density at 7.9 is `r f2(dnorm(7.9, 7.9, 0.02))`. A colleague says
   the model must be wrong, because no probability can exceed 1. What
   would you tell them?
2. Genetic mark-recapture studies identify each bear from a genotype
   in a hair sample. Suppose two unrelated bears share a genotype by
   chance with probability 1 in 10,000. A study genotypes 150 bears.
   How worried should the study be that two different bears get the
   same ID, and what would you change in the study if the answer were
   "very"?

## Bonus: computing on the log scale {#log-scale-birthday}

The birthday probability can also be written with factorials:

$$P(\text{all different}) = \frac{365!}{(365 - n)! \, 365^n}.$$

Typed directly into R, this fails, because $365!$ is far beyond the
largest number a computer stores:

```{r factorial-overflow}
factorial(365)
365^25
```

The fix is to work with logarithms, where products become sums and
huge numbers become manageable. `lfactorial()` returns $\log(n!)$
without ever computing $n!$:

```{r log-scale}
log_p <- lfactorial(365) - lfactorial(365 - 25) - 25 * log(365)
exp(log_p)
p_all_diff
```

Working on the log scale and exponentiating only at the end is a habit
worth forming. Products of many small probabilities run into the
opposite problem (they round to zero), and that happens every time we
multiply the probabilities of many data points together, which we will
do constantly later in the semester.

# Probability distributions {#distributions}

A named distribution is a model for the noise in data, and each comes
with a story about how the data arose. This part opens with the WOD on
the sample mean, then covers R's four functions for every distribution,
the discrete and continuous distributions used most in ecology, and
how to choose among them from the process that generated the data.

## 1. WOD: expectation and the sample mean {#wod-sample-mean}

The WOD used brook trout lengths with mean $\mu = 22$ cm and variance
$\sigma^2 = 16$ cm². The population mean $\mu$ is a fixed number (a
**parameter**). The average $\bar{x}$ of 5 trout you catch is a
**statistic**: catch a different 5 and it changes, so it is a random
variable with its own distribution.

For $n$ independent measurements, $\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum X_i$, and
the rules from [section 6](#moments) give

$$E[\bar{X}] = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n E[X_i] = \mu, \qquad
\text{Var}(\bar{X}) = \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{i=1}^n \text{Var}(X_i) =
\frac{\sigma^2}{n}.$$

The second step adds the variances, which requires the measurements to
be independent. The standard deviation of $\bar{X}$ (the **standard
error**) is $\sigma / \sqrt{n}$: four times as many fish halve it.

Simulation confirms the algebra. Draw 10,000 samples of 5 trout and
look at the spread of their means:

```{r sample-means}
set.seed(746)
xbar_5 <- replicate(10000, mean(rnorm(5, mean = 22, sd = 4)))
var(xbar_5)        # theory: 16 / 5 = 3.2
sd(xbar_5)         # theory: 4 / sqrt(5)
```

```{r sample-mean-hist, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=2.9}
set.seed(747)
xbar_list <- list(rnorm(10000, 22, 4),
                  xbar_5,
                  replicate(10000, mean(rnorm(20, 22, 4))))
labs <- c("n = 1 (single fish)", "n = 5", "n = 20")
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 0.5))
for (j in 1:3) {
  hist(xbar_list[[j]], breaks = seq(0, 44, by = 0.5), xlim = c(8, 36),
       col = "grey80", border = "white", main = labs[j],
       xlab = "Mean length (cm)", freq = FALSE)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

> **Question:** The variance formula assumed the five trout were
> independent. Suppose all five came from one pool, where fish share
> food and temperature and so resemble each other. Would the variance
> of $\bar{x}$ be larger or smaller than $\sigma^2/5$? Why?

## 2. Four functions for every distribution {#dpqr}

R gives every distribution four functions, named by a prefix:

```{r dpqr-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Prefix = c("`d`", "`p`", "`q`", "`r`"),
  Returns = c("probability (pmf) or density (pdf) at x",
              "cumulative probability, P(X ≤ x)",
              "quantile: the x with P(X ≤ x) equal to a given probability",
              "random draws"),
  `Trout example` = c("`dnorm(22, 22, 4)`", "`pnorm(30, 22, 4)`",
                      "`qnorm(0.9, 22, 4)`", "`rnorm(5, 22, 4)`"),
  check.names = FALSE))
```

```{r dpqr}
dnorm(22, mean = 22, sd = 4)         # density at 22 cm
1 - pnorm(30, mean = 22, sd = 4)     # P(a trout is longer than 30 cm)
qnorm(0.9, mean = 22, sd = 4)        # 90% of trout are shorter than this
set.seed(1)
rnorm(5, mean = 22, sd = 4)          # five simulated trout
```

```{r dpqr-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=2.9}
par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 0.5))
curve(dnorm(x, 22, 4), 8, 36, lwd = 2, xlab = "Length (cm)", ylab = "Density",
      main = "d: density")
segments(22, 0, 22, dnorm(22, 22, 4), lty = 2)
curve(pnorm(x, 22, 4), 8, 36, lwd = 2, xlab = "Length (cm)",
      ylab = "P(X ≤ x)", main = "p: cumulative")
segments(30, 0, 30, pnorm(30, 22, 4), lty = 2)
segments(8, pnorm(30, 22, 4), 30, pnorm(30, 22, 4), lty = 2)
curve(pnorm(x, 22, 4), 8, 36, lwd = 2, xlab = "Length (cm)",
      ylab = "P(X ≤ x)", main = "q: quantile")
segments(8, 0.9, qnorm(0.9, 22, 4), 0.9, lty = 2)
arrows(qnorm(0.9, 22, 4), 0.9, qnorm(0.9, 22, 4), 0, lty = 2, length = 0.07)
set.seed(2)
hist(rnorm(1000, 22, 4), breaks = 30, col = "grey80", border = "white",
     xlim = c(8, 36), xlab = "Length (cm)", main = "r: 1000 draws")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

About `r round(100 * (1 - pnorm(30, 22, 4)), 1)`% of trout are longer than 30 cm, and
90% are shorter than `r f2(qnorm(0.9, 22, 4))` cm. The `q` function
runs the `p` function backward. For discrete distributions, `p`
includes the value itself: `pbinom(2, 6, 0.25)` is $P(X \le 2)$, so
$P(X \ge 3)$ is `1 - pbinom(2, 6, 0.25)`.

## 3. Discrete distributions {#discrete}

**Binomial**, $X \sim \text{Binom}(N, p)$: the number of successes in
$N$ independent trials, each with the same probability $p$ (Bolker
4.5.1.1). Mean $Np$, variance $Np(1 - p)$. Use it when there is a known
upper limit: nests that fail out of nests monitored, seeds taken out of
seeds offered, infected frogs out of frogs swabbed. With $N = 1$ it is
called a Bernoulli trial.

**Poisson**, $X \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda)$: counts of independent
events in a fixed area or time at a constant rate, with no upper limit
(seeds per quadrat, birds per point count). Its single parameter is
both the mean and the variance:

$$P(X = x) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!}, \qquad E[X] = \text{Var}(X) = \lambda.$$

It is also the limit of the binomial when $N$ is large and $p$ small
with $Np = \lambda$ fixed.

**Negative binomial**, $X \sim \text{NegBin}(\mu, k)$: counts that
vary more than a Poisson allows, often because individuals are
clumped. Bolker's parameterization (R's `mu` and `size`) has mean $\mu$
and variance $\mu + \mu^2/k$. Small $k$ means strong clumping; as $k$
grows, the negative binomial approaches the Poisson. The **geometric**
distribution (number of failures before the first success) is a
negative binomial with $k = 1$.

Seeds per quadrat with a mean of 4, Poisson versus clumped:

```{r pois-nb-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.2}
x_seed <- 0:15
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 0.5))
pmf_plot(x_seed, dpois(x_seed, 4), xlab = "Seeds per quadrat",
         main = "Poisson(4)", ylim = c(0, 0.22))
pmf_plot(x_seed, dnbinom(x_seed, mu = 4, size = 1.5), xlab = "Seeds per quadrat",
         main = "NegBin(4, k = 1.5)", ylim = c(0, 0.22))
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The red triangles mark the means, both 4.

```{r pois-nb}
c(poisson = 4, negbin = 4 + 4^2 / 1.5)                             # variances
c(poisson = dpois(0, 4), negbin = dnbinom(0, mu = 4, size = 1.5))  # P(no seeds)
```

The two have the same mean, but the negative binomial has variance
`r f2(4 + 16 / 1.5)` instead of 4, and
`r round(dnbinom(0, mu = 4, size = 1.5) / dpois(0, 4), 1)` times as many
empty quadrats.

## 4. Continuous distributions {#continuous}

**Normal**, $X \sim \text{Normal}(\mu, \sigma)$: symmetric and
unbounded. Its two parameters are its mean and standard deviation, and
its variance does not change with its mean. Averages and sums of many
independent pieces tend toward a normal distribution (the central limit
theorem), which is why the sample means above looked bell-shaped even
for $n = 5$.

**Gamma**, $X \sim \text{Gamma}(a, s)$: positive and right-skewed
(Bolker 4.5.2.3), for quantities like biomass or rainfall. With shape
$a$ and scale $s$, the mean is $as$ and the variance $as^2$, so the
standard deviation grows in proportion to the mean (CV $= 1/\sqrt{a}$).
In R, use `dgamma(x, shape = a, scale = s)`; the default second
argument is the *rate*, $1/s$.

**Exponential**, $X \sim \text{Exp}(r)$: the waiting time between
independent events that occur at rate $r$, and a gamma with shape 1.
Mean $1/r$.

**Lognormal**: positive and right-skewed; $\log X$ is normal. Like the
gamma, its standard deviation grows with its mean. It gets a full
treatment with [trends on the log scale](Week5_SimulatingData.html#lognormal).

**Beta**, $X \sim \text{Beta}(a, b)$: proportions and probabilities,
between 0 and 1 (fraction of a quadrat covered, a survival
probability). Mean $a/(a + b)$. The beta is also the usual choice for a
prior distribution on a probability.

```{r continuous-shapes, fig.width=9, fig.height=2.9}
par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 0.5))
curve(dgamma(x, shape = 2, scale = 2), 0, 15, lwd = 2, xlab = "Biomass (g)",
      ylab = "Density", main = "Gamma(a = 2, s = 2)")
curve(dexp(x, rate = 1.5), 0, 4, lwd = 2, xlab = "Hours between visits",
      ylab = "Density", main = "Exponential(1.5)")
curve(dlnorm(x, meanlog = 2, sdlog = 0.5), 0, 25, lwd = 2, xlab = "Body mass (g)",
      ylab = "Density", main = "Lognormal(2, 0.5)")
curve(dbeta(x, 2, 5), 0, 1, lwd = 2, xlab = "Proportion cover",
      ylab = "Density", main = "Beta(2, 5)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The widget plots each distribution for any parameter values, marks the
mean and one standard deviation either side, and reports the variance
to mean ratio and CV. "Draw 200 values" overlays a random sample.

```{r explorer-widget, echo=FALSE}
widget("distribution_explorer.html")
```

> **Question:** Choose Poisson and move $\lambda$ from 1 to 20 while
> watching the "Variance / mean" card. Then choose Negative binomial,
> set the mean to 4, and move $k$ from 0.5 to 20. Which distribution
> could describe counts whose variance is 3.5 times their mean, and
> roughly what $k$ would it need?

## 5. Choosing a distribution {#choosing}

Choose a distribution from the process that generated the data, not
from the shape of a histogram. Bolker's bestiary (section 4.5)
describes each distribution by the mechanism behind it for this
reason. A few questions narrow the choice quickly:

- **Counts or measurements?** Counts are discrete; lengths, masses, and
  concentrations are continuous.
- **What values are possible?** Is there a lower bound (zero), an upper
  bound (the number of trials, or 1 for a proportion)?
- **How should the spread change with the mean?** Constant (normal),
  equal to the mean (Poisson), faster than the mean (negative binomial),
  or proportional to the mean (gamma, lognormal)?

```{r choosing-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Data = c("successes out of a known number of trials",
           "counts with no fixed upper limit, events independent",
           "counts with no fixed upper limit, clumped or overdispersed",
           "continuous, symmetric, can be negative",
           "continuous, positive, right-skewed",
           "waiting times between independent events",
           "proportions or probabilities between 0 and 1"),
  Consider = c("binomial", "Poisson", "negative binomial", "normal",
               "gamma or lognormal", "exponential", "beta")))
```

**Checking the mean-variance relationship.** Here are seed counts from
20 quadrats (simulated):

```{r seed-counts}
set.seed(14)
seeds <- rnbinom(20, mu = 4, size = 1.5)
seeds
c(mean = mean(seeds), variance = var(seeds), ratio = var(seeds) / mean(seeds))
```

A Poisson would have a variance-to-mean ratio near 1; these counts
have `r f2(var(seeds) / mean(seeds))`. A quick estimate of the negative
binomial's $k$ matches the sample moments to the theoretical ones (the
**method of moments**, Bolker 4.4.6): set $\bar{x} = \mu$ and
$s^2 = \mu + \mu^2/k$, then solve for $k$:

$$\hat{k} = \frac{\bar{x}}{s^2/\bar{x} - 1}.$$

```{r method-of-moments}
m <- mean(seeds)
k_hat <- m / (var(seeds) / m - 1)
k_hat
```

```{r method-of-moments-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.4}
x_q <- 0:16
obs <- table(factor(seeds, levels = x_q))
par(mar = c(4, 4, 0.5, 0.5))
mids <- barplot(obs, col = "grey80", border = NA, ylim = c(0, 5),
                xlab = "Seeds per quadrat", ylab = "Number of quadrats")
points(mids, 20 * dpois(x_q, m), pch = 16, type = "b", lty = 2)
points(mids, 20 * dnbinom(x_q, mu = m, size = k_hat), pch = 17, type = "b",
       col = "firebrick")
legend("topright", c("Poisson", "negative binomial"), pch = c(16, 17),
       lty = c(2, 1), col = c("black", "firebrick"), bty = "n")
```

The Poisson expects almost every quadrat to hold 2 to 6 seeds, and
gives the quadrat with `r max(seeds)` seeds a probability of about
`r round(1e6 * dpois(max(seeds), m))` in a million. The negative binomial with
$\hat{k} =$ `r f2(k_hat)` spreads its probability over the low counts
and the long right tail, where these data are. The method of moments gives a first
estimate; maximum likelihood (later in the semester) is the better
tool.

## Discussion

1. A colleague models clutch size, which in this species is always 2
   to 5 eggs, as Poisson with mean 3.4. What does this model get wrong
   about the possible values? What would you check in the data?
2. The quadrat seed counts had a variance about 3.5 times their mean.
   Name two ecological processes that could produce the extra
   variance. How would each one appear in a data-generating model?
3. Herbivore damage is measured on 50 leaves. One student proposes a
   beta distribution for the fraction of leaf area eaten; another
   proposes a binomial. What would each student have to believe about
   how the data were collected?

## Bonus: where the negative binomial comes from {#compounding}

One way to get clumped counts: each quadrat has its own seed rate
$\lambda_i$ (some sit under a parent plant, some don't), and seeds
within a quadrat are Poisson around that rate. If the rates vary as a
gamma distribution with mean $\mu$ and shape $k$, the resulting counts
are exactly negative binomial with mean $\mu$ and overdispersion $k$
(Bolker 4.6.3, where he notes it could be called the gamma-Poisson
distribution):

$$\lambda_i \sim \text{Gamma}(k, \mu/k), \qquad Y_i \sim
\text{Pois}(\lambda_i) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad Y_i \sim
\text{NegBin}(\mu, k).$$

```{r compounding}
set.seed(5)
rates <- rgamma(10000, shape = 1.5, scale = 4 / 1.5)   # quadrat-to-quadrat variation
y_mix <- rpois(10000, rates)
c(mean = mean(y_mix), variance = var(y_mix))          # NegBin: 4 and 4 + 4^2 / 1.5
```

```{r compounding-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.4}
x_c <- 0:20
par(mar = c(4, 4, 0.5, 0.5))
mids <- barplot(table(factor(y_mix, levels = x_c)) / 10000, col = "grey80",
                border = NA, ylim = c(0, 0.17), xlab = "Seeds per quadrat",
                ylab = "Proportion")
points(mids, dnbinom(x_c, mu = 4, size = 1.5), pch = 17, col = "firebrick")
legend("topright", c("gamma-Poisson simulation", "NegBin(4, k = 1.5)"),
       fill = c("grey80", NA), border = NA, pch = c(NA, 17),
       col = c(NA, "firebrick"), bty = "n")
```

The bars (simulation) and triangles (`dnbinom()`) agree. This gives
$k$ a meaning: it is the shape of the distribution of rates among
quadrats, so a small $k$ says the quadrats differ a lot in their
underlying rate. Overdispersion in counts is often a sign of unmeasured
variation among sampling units, a theme that returns with random
effects later in the semester.
